title: 3 leadership frameworks actually worth paying attention to
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez, writing from an education background, argues that not all approaches to leading are equally good and that celebrating variety can excuse avoidant behavior. She defines good leadership as unrelenting reflection, self-awareness and willingness to change, then offers three frameworks she finds transformative. Learning-centered leadership (Senge) builds collective learning, servant leadership flips the org chart toward listening and support, and situational leadership demands adaptability backed by self-awareness. She notes what unites them: they are human-centered, accountable and relational. The practical takeaway is to ask what people need and how actions will land.
points: Variability in leadership should not be an excuse: authentic differences in approach are healthy, but avoiding feedback and accountability is not.
Learning-centered leadership treats the leader as steward of the team's collective growth, which is slow and invisible but shifts culture over time.
Servant leadership is radical because it decentralizes power, requiring more listening than talking and more supporting than controlling.
Situational leadership is organized common sense, and it only works when leaders do the self-reflection to know their own blindspots.
All three frameworks reduce to a few questions: what do my people need, how will my actions land, and what does this moment call for.
quotes: Honest, strong, impactful, and-simply put- good leadership is centered around absolutely unrelenting reflection. It’s pausing to examine our every pattern of doing and thinking. It’s being deeply self-aware about how we engage with and impact other humans. It’s being so willing to be challenged-to stay in the room when things get uncomfortable, or when you’ve done something wrong. Most importantly, good leadership requires change. It’s not about preserving our preferences and comforts, but evolving our capacity to support others.

What really resonates for me about learning-center leadership is that it’s less about control, power, and authority and more about stewardship-stewarding growth, learning, possibility, and sustainability. It’s not flashy. For those of us who sometimes act like squirrels-chasing every goddamn new thing or possible quick win that catches our attention-it’s slow, and often invisible. But I can promise you that it’s the kind of leadership that shifts culture over time.

Servant leadership flips the traditional org chart. Instead of the leader being at the top, they position themselves as the bottom-they’re the foundation, the building blocks, supporting the people and systems around them. Contrary to top-down leadership structures, it requires more listening than talking. More asking than directing. More supporting than controlling. Servant leaders often position themselves on the ground, at the back of the line, making sure no one gets left behind.

Situational leaders must be incredibly self-aware, mindful of how their actions (and lack thereof) impact others. In fast-based organizational contexts, this might be hard, because it means the leader must intentionally carve out time for reflection, pause, and inquiry.

Common sense is often said but it really functions as an unwritten social code, totally absent of clarity. Leaders are only human. They’re like everyone else in that they are influenced by blindspots, habits, traumas, and more. Without a shared framework for what “common sense” means, and an expectation that leaders do the work of enhancing their emotional intelligence, we leave space for situational leadership to fall short, even when it doesn’t need to.
